Introduction

Ziqian XIONG is a Computer Science undergraduate at UNNC and our team leader. His medical image segmentation research involves model implementation, dataset checks, and comparative evaluation. His 4DGS tool and MomoFocus application provide Python/Flask and React/TypeScript development experience. For P19, these experiences provide a basis for comparing skill-matching and ranking methods and connecting them to an interactive recommendation application. Personal website: https://qqqqqprofile.vercel.app/.

Internship Experience

  • Pony.ai algorithm internship (July–September 2026): In the AI department, investigated VGGT-related 3D/4D reconstruction methods and compared multi-view geometry and depth estimation against an existing DA3/3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline. Completed feasibility validation and engineering integration, replacing the original reconstruction workflow. Also wrote documentation on agent-assisted development workflows.

Project Experience

  • 4DGS-Edit-and-Compare (July–September 2026): Independently developed a 4D Gaussian Splatting point-cloud editing and comparison tool. It supports rotation, translation, and deletion of selected regions, editing and comparing multiple point clouds, and quantitative evaluation. Technology stack: Python/Flask for the backend, JavaScript/Three.js/WebGL for the interactive frontend, NumPy/SciPy for numerical processing, PyTorch/plyfile for point-cloud file handling, and Docker for packaging. Developed independently during the Pony.ai internship, the tool is reported on his website as being used by the company. Project repository.

  • MomoFocus (September–October 2026): Developed a personal productivity application integrating to-do lists, notes, and a Pomodoro timer. Technology stack: React, TypeScript, and CSS for the interface; Electron for the desktop shell; Vite for development and frontend builds; and electron-builder for desktop packaging. The implementation uses localStorage for local persistence and dnd-kit for sortable lists, providing relevant experience in interactive application development and desktop delivery. Project repository.

Research Experience

  • Medical image segmentation research: Implemented and debugged CNN–Transformer components; prepared and checked datasets; evaluated Dice, IoU, and inference speed. Technology stack: Python, PyTorch, and OpenMMLab's MMSegmentation, MMCV, and MMEngine. A related paper is under submission to CVIU with him as second author.

  • Dynamic dual-branch neural network research: Investigating a multi-task network for keyword spotting and speaker verification, with early-exit scheduling and FPGA resource reallocation. Network design, scheduling, and resource-allocation strategies remain under evaluation.

Skill Set

  • Programming languages: Python, C/C++, Java, Haskell, JavaScript, TypeScript, Lean, and Verilog.

  • Databases: MySQL.

  • Research and implementation: PyTorch; OpenMMLab (MMSegmentation, MMCV, and MMEngine); CNN–Transformer models; data preprocessing and comparative model evaluation; Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

  • Application development: HTML, CSS, React, Electron, Vite, Flask, Three.js/WebGL, NumPy, and SciPy.

  • Engineering and documentation: Docker packaging, electron-builder, and technical documentation for agent-assisted development workflows, including harness and loop engineering.

phases.title: Requirements & data audit
tasks: Agree student journeys, acceptance criteria, authorised recruitment-data access, and the initial Zhejiang subset. Audit sample fields, dates, missing values, and duplicate records; draft the data dictionary and evaluation split.

Measure sample-processing memory and runtime, and prepare storage/compute requests from 21 October. Submit ethics forms by 28 October, covering student profiles, feedback, consent, and planned user trials; begin participant work only after the required approval.

phases.title: Cleaning & matching baseline
tasks: Publish the team project website by 5 November, with the project scope, team roles, and progress plan. Design Parquet/DuckDB data storage, profile tables, and FastAPI contracts; use synthetic profiles for interface development.

Implement batch cleaning, salary-period normalisation, cross-platform deduplication, skill dictionaries, and keyword matching. Deliver a queryable authorised subset, quality statistics, and a reproducible recommendation baseline by 24 November. Prepare interface skeletons and reusable evaluation fixtures in parallel with this baseline.

phases.title: First workflow & pilot comparisons
tasks: Implement salary, growth, stability, and skill-fit scoring, chronological trend baselines, and a queryable occupation–skill graph. By 15 December, demonstrate profile entry, qualification/location filters, adjustable weights, ranked jobs, matched skills, skill gaps, and explanations on an authorised subset.

In parallel, prepare React/TypeScript and FastAPI interface skeletons, a minimal explicit-feedback example, and pilot keyword, skill-only, and semantic comparisons with reusable evaluation scripts. Submit the interim report by 10 December, using evidence available then; archive code/data versions and integration issues by 15 December.

phases.title: Document review & earlier tasks
tasks: Use this time to review documents, collect feedback, and finish earlier tasks as needed; no critical work or participant trials are scheduled. Low-workload activity continues from 6 January.

phases.title: Low-workload review & documentation
tasks: Review existing skill dictionaries, data-quality notes, score explanations, and saved pilot results in small independent tasks; draft the API and user guides. These tasks must not block the March workflow.

Use asynchronous check-ins to maintain the issue list and prepare test labels, trial instructions, and March priorities from existing materials. Make no full-application delivery commitment in January or February; resume concentrated integration on 1 March.

phases.title: Web & feedback integration
tasks: Complete the existing profile, ranking, score-breakdown, and graph views, keeping data dates and coverage visible. Connect saved preferences, favourites, and explicit feedback to reversible, user-approved weight updates; finalise versioned API and scoring records.
By 9 March, demonstrate entry, recommendation, explanation, feedback, and refresh. Admit semantic matching only if the pilot supports it; keep a working baseline and add no complex model scope.

phases.title: Evaluation & student trials
tasks: Use the prepared chronological splits, labels, and scripts to compare keyword, skill-only, and hybrid ranking with HR@k, NDCG, and MRR. Review skill extraction, trend errors, graph usefulness, and the contribution of each quality dimension.

Run approved student trials and latency/resource checks in parallel; prioritise explanation clarity, empty results, and abnormal weights. Complete the evaluation report and essential fixes by 16 March.

phases.title: Release, report & demonstration
tasks: Freeze features and models on 17 March, regress core journeys, and verify Docker deployment in a fresh environment by 23 March. Reproduce representative evaluation results and complete authorised-data access, configuration, limitation, and user instructions.

Use 24–30 March to rehearse weight changes, skill gaps, and career-path demonstrations; complete the software release, source repository, final report, user guide, and demonstration materials by 30 March.

phases.title: Submission checks
tasks: Verify release/report/documentation consistency, filenames, access, and receipts; submit the team final report and software by 1 April. Prepare demonstration, presentation, and promotional assets for later course submissions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.html:
Project: SmartCareer: A Personalized Employment Recommendation System with a Multi-Dimensional Job Quality Evaluation Model

UNNC GRP Team202610 brings together experience in data preparation, model evaluation, and interactive software development that fits SmartCareer's main challenges. Yun Xin NG's data-engineering internship and machine-learning projects support working with recruitment data, while Ziqian XIONG's model experiments and Flask/React projects provide a basis for connecting recommendation methods with a usable application. Research annotation, programming, database, and CI/CD skills across the team complement these experiences.

As university students, we want to help our peers understand why a job suits them and which skills they could develop. We will combine student profiles and skill matching with transparent scores for salary, growth, stability, and skill fit, so that users can explore how their priorities change the recommendations.

Led by Ziqian XIONG, we will first demonstrate an explainable recommendation workflow on the Zhejiang graduate subset, then evaluate trend forecasting, occupation relationships, and ranking improvements. Shared learning, regular integration, and early supervisor feedback will help us turn our complementary preparation into a working system. We will assess recommendations through baseline comparisons and student trials, and clearly show the dates and limitations of historical job data.

sections.title: Teammates
sections.html:
Our seven-member team, led by Ziqian XIONG, combines data preparation and model evaluation, algorithm implementation, application and database development, and testing, deployment, and user communication. We will connect these strengths through shared data definitions, module interfaces, and integration reviews so that experimental results become demonstrable software. The following profiles present the experience supporting our project plan; responsibilities are set out in the work-distribution section.

We believe that the bidding groups have broadly comparable academic foundations. We therefore see stronger leadership and proactive engagement as our competitive advantage: a leader who can guide shared learning and coordinate decisions, and members willing to investigate unfamiliar methods, raise difficulties early, and follow through on feedback. We will put this into practice through weekly progress reviews during concentrated development, paired method discussions, and early demonstrations; the low-workload period will use brief asynchronous check-ins.

  • From a transparent baseline to a usable service: Ziqian XIONG's comparative model evaluation, Yue WU's Python/SQLite and analysis background, and Xinyun HU's programming and database foundations provide a basis for developing and checking skill matching, quality scoring, and profile-to-result workflows. Oswald Yiwen CHONG can support GitHub collaboration, automated checks, and deployment; Jinyao LU can support student-facing requirements, trials, and demonstrations.

  • A focused seven-person delivery structure: We will organise data, algorithms, and application workstreams with explicit handovers and shared integration checkpoints. We will first demonstrate a transparent baseline on the Zhejiang graduate subset, then evaluate trends, graph features, and ranking improvements. Our seven members will share implementation and review across these three workstreams, with one leader coordinating interfaces and delivery.

sections.title: Ideas & Design
sections.html:
Project Proposal

SmartCareer will help students understand which occupations fit their skills, why a job is recommended, and which skills they need to develop. Students will enter their major, skills, qualifications, location, and career priorities, adjust the importance of salary, growth, stability, and skill fit, and receive ranked jobs with dimension scores, explanations, and skill gaps. An occupation–skill graph will show related career pathways, while explicit relevance feedback will support user-approved preference updates.

Development will begin with the Zhejiang graduate subset of the research group's recruitment data and scale through batch processing. Historical records will support labour-market analysis and recommendation evaluation; the interface will display their dates and distinguish them from current vacancies. The core deliverables are a clean queryable dataset, skill dictionary and new-occupation graph, documented quality model, evaluated recommendation module, working web application, and final report, source code, and demonstration.

Technology Stack & System Design

  1. Back-end Development

    Python and pandas will clean records in batches, standardise salary periods and ranges, remove cross-platform duplicates, and preserve source and transformation records. Parquet will hold offline features, DuckDB will query recruitment data, and SQLite will store student profiles, preferences, and feedback. FastAPI will expose profile, search, recommendation, explanation, graph, and feedback endpoints.

    Skill dictionaries and synonym rules will provide an extraction baseline. scikit-learn will support keyword and skill matching, hybrid ranking, and forecasting comparisons. Monthly or quarterly skill shares will feed seasonal-naive and lag-feature regression forecasts, evaluated using chronological splits. NetworkX will represent occupation–skill relationships; persistent changes in titles, skill combinations, and demand will identify candidate emerging occupations for manual review.

    The four quality dimensions will use comparable salary percentiles, demand and skill trends, demand persistence and variation, and student–job skill fit. Growth and stability will be labelled as proxy measures. Non-negative weights will sum to one; missing dimensions will be shown and handled through explicit coverage rules. Hybrid ranking will combine matching and quality scores without counting skill fit twice. Explanations will use the actual scores and matched skills. Keyword, skill-only, and hybrid approaches will be compared using HR@k, NDCG, MRR, and student trials.

  2. Front-end Development

    React and TypeScript will provide profile entry, region and qualification filters, weight controls, ranked results, score breakdowns, skill-gap views, occupation relationships, and feedback. The interface will call FastAPI through documented JSON contracts and show data dates, coverage, and empty-result guidance. Preference changes will be visible and reversible.

Engineering and delivery: GitHub reviews and automated checks will cover cleaning, score calculations, ranking, and API integration. Docker will package the application. Versioned data, dictionaries, scoring configurations, and evaluation splits will make recommendations reproducible. Our seven members will work across data, algorithms, and application delivery, with paired review connecting these workstreams.

Core data flow: Authorised recruitment data → cleaning and skill extraction → Parquet/DuckDB features → trends and occupation graph → profile-based matching and quality scoring → ranked explanations → user feedback.

Ziqian XIONG will lead weekly progress and integration reviews during concentrated development and use brief asynchronous check-ins in the low-workload period. Paired discussions of methods and code, and early demonstrations, will support supervisor feedback. The leader will help members break down unfamiliar tasks and resolve dependencies. Each member will prepare questions, report blockers early, and record decisions and follow-up actions.

The project runs from 21 October 2026 to final submission on 1 April 2027, with work organised by date ranges, workload, and demonstrable outputs. We use 16 December 2026–5 January 2027 to review documents and finish earlier tasks as needed. As January and February may overlap the winter vacation, 6 January–28 February is a low-workload period: at most one small asynchronous task per member per week, adjusted to availability, with no critical integration, required training runs, or participant trials. University holiday dates remain subject to formal notices. We bring the first demonstrable workflow and pilot experiments forward to 15 December, complete integration and evaluation in March, and reserve 31 March–1 April for submission checks.

Course milestones follow the supplied tentative key-dates table, subject to formal course notices.

  • 21 October – 3 November 2026

    • Agree student journeys, acceptance criteria, authorised recruitment-data access, and the initial Zhejiang subset. Audit sample fields, dates, missing values, and duplicate records; draft the data dictionary and evaluation split.

    • Measure sample-processing memory and runtime, and prepare storage/compute requests from 21 October. Submit ethics forms by 28 October, covering student profiles, feedback, consent, and planned user trials; begin participant work only after the required approval.

  • 4–24 November 2026

    • Publish the team project website by 5 November, with the project scope, team roles, and progress plan. Design Parquet/DuckDB data storage, profile tables, and FastAPI contracts; use synthetic profiles for interface development.

    • Implement batch cleaning, salary-period normalisation, cross-platform deduplication, skill dictionaries, and keyword matching. Deliver a queryable authorised subset, quality statistics, and a reproducible recommendation baseline by 24 November. Prepare interface skeletons and reusable evaluation fixtures in parallel with this baseline.

  • 25 November – 15 December 2026

    • Implement salary, growth, stability, and skill-fit scoring, chronological trend baselines, and a queryable occupation–skill graph. By 15 December, demonstrate profile entry, qualification/location filters, adjustable weights, ranked jobs, matched skills, skill gaps, and explanations on an authorised subset.

    • In parallel, prepare React/TypeScript and FastAPI interface skeletons, a minimal explicit-feedback example, and pilot keyword, skill-only, and semantic comparisons with reusable evaluation scripts. Submit the interim report by 10 December, using evidence available then; archive code/data versions and integration issues by 15 December.

  • 16 December 2026 – 5 January 2027

    • Use this time to review documents, collect feedback, and finish earlier tasks as needed; no critical work or participant trials are scheduled. Low-workload activity continues from 6 January.

  • 6 January – 28 February 2027

    • Review existing skill dictionaries, data-quality notes, score explanations, and saved pilot results in small independent tasks; draft the API and user guides. These tasks must not block the March workflow.

    • Use asynchronous check-ins to maintain the issue list and prepare test labels, trial instructions, and March priorities from existing materials. Make no full-application delivery commitment in January or February; resume concentrated integration on 1 March.

  • 1–9 March 2027

    • Complete the existing profile, ranking, score-breakdown, and graph views, keeping data dates and coverage visible. Connect saved preferences, favourites, and explicit feedback to reversible, user-approved weight updates; finalise versioned API and scoring records.

    • By 9 March, demonstrate entry, recommendation, explanation, feedback, and refresh. Admit semantic matching only if the pilot supports it; keep a working baseline and add no complex model scope.

  • 10–16 March 2027

    • Use the prepared chronological splits, labels, and scripts to compare keyword, skill-only, and hybrid ranking with HR@k, NDCG, and MRR. Review skill extraction, trend errors, graph usefulness, and the contribution of each quality dimension.

    • Run approved student trials and latency/resource checks in parallel; prioritise explanation clarity, empty results, and abnormal weights. Complete the evaluation report and essential fixes by 16 March.

  • 17–30 March 2027

    • Freeze features and models on 17 March, regress core journeys, and verify Docker deployment in a fresh environment by 23 March. Reproduce representative evaluation results and complete authorised-data access, configuration, limitation, and user instructions.

    • Use 24–30 March to rehearse weight changes, skill gaps, and career-path demonstrations; complete the software release, source repository, final report, user guide, and demonstration materials by 30 March.

  • 31 March – 1 April 2027

    • Verify release/report/documentation consistency, filenames, access, and receipts; submit the team final report and software by 1 April. Prepare demonstration, presentation, and promotional assets for later course submissions.

Work Distribution

We will divide the work according to our relevant experience and interests, help one another learn unfamiliar methods, and adjust tasks through progress discussions and supervisor feedback.

  • Ziqian XIONG: Coordinate the team and supervisor discussions; guide system design, skill matching, ranking experiments, and model integration, drawing on his research and software projects.

  • Yun Xin NG: Prepare and clean recruitment data, normalise salary fields, and develop skill-trend forecasts, drawing on her data-engineering and machine-learning experience.

  • Jinyao LU: Organise student requirements and trials, check whether recommendation explanations are understandable, and prepare user documentation and demonstrations.

  • Oswald Yiwen CHONG: Develop backend services and connect application modules; support GitHub collaboration, automated checks, and deployment using his application-development and CI/CD experience.

  • Ziqian ZHANG: Prepare checked skill and occupation samples, organise annotations, and record data and recommendation errors, building on her research data-preparation experience.

  • Yue WU: Develop skill-normalisation rules, four-dimensional scoring, and occupation relationships; compare methods and document the reasoning behind scores.

  • Xinyun HU: Build student-profile, preference, and recommendation pages; connect them to backend services and check filtering, weight changes, and feedback interactions.

Yun Xin NG and Ziqian ZHANG will check data samples together; Yue WU and Ziqian XIONG will discuss scoring and ranking results. The application and user-trial work will connect these results to the student experience.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.html:
SmartCareer needs a team that can connect real recruitment data, transparent evaluation, and a usable student application. Our complementary preparation in data extraction, model experiments, programming, databases, delivery automation, and user coordination provides a credible basis for that work. We will demonstrate a reproducible baseline first, then use ranking metrics and student trials to justify improvements. This makes our bid a practical route from an available dataset to an explainable employment-support tool.

Building on our academic preparation, we aim to distinguish our team through stronger leadership and peer guidance, proactive learning, and consistent follow-through throughout the project.
